e.t: Kenan is a personal name, referring to a man in the genealogical records of Genesis and 1 Chronicles. It identifies the descendant of Enosh and the ancestor of Mahalalel, appearing within the family line recorded in Genesis 5. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, with five occurrences in Genesis and one in 1 Chronicles. Scripture presents it as a person’s name rather than as a descriptive word or action.

gl: Rogelim , a place East of the Jordan
d: Rogelim , a place East of the Jordan

e.t: Rogelim is a Hebrew place-name, rendered “Rogelim.” It identifies a geographic location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in 2 Samuel: 2 Samuel 17:27 and 2 Samuel 19:31. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself supports identifying the place, but not adding details about its location, history, or role in those passages.

This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Rezon.” It refers to an individual rather than expressing a general quality, action, or concept. The name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Kings 11:23. Because the available wording identifies the person’s name but does not provide a separate lexical definition, its ordinary meaning is simply the proper name Rezon. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s role or significance in the passage.

This Hebrew word means “long.” It describes something extended rather than short, whether the surrounding sentence concerns measure, distance, duration, or another kind of extension. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its normal meaning is clear but its precise force depends on the sentence where it appears. One recorded rendering presents it as “long,” supporting this straightforward sense without requiring a broader or different definition.

This Hebrew word describes the action expressed by “signed”: putting one’s name or authority onto a written decree or document. It functions as a verb, showing what someone does rather than naming an object. In its seven Old Testament occurrences, all in Daniel, it concerns written royal commands and their formal authorization. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage. The word appears in Daniel 5:24–25 and Daniel 6:8–13.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in the book of Job. The available passages are Job 36:26 and Job 37:23, but the verse wording is not included here, so its precise nuance cannot be stated responsibly beyond this basic description. It should therefore be understood by reading the surrounding sentences in each passage rather than by assigning it an unsupported range of meanings.

This Hebrew word means “garlic,” naming the pungent edible bulb used as food. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Numbers 11:5. Its role is concrete and specific rather than a broad description or abstract idea: it identifies a particular food. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear and limited to garlic.

“Knife” is a cutting tool used as a noun. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word appears once, rendered “knife,” so its meaning is narrow and concrete rather than a broad description of a person, quality, or action. It names a sharp-edged implement used for cutting in ordinary use. Its only recorded occurrence is Proverbs 23:2; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular role in that sentence.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to thorny briars—rough, unwanted growth that can overtake cultivated land. It appears 11 times in the Old Testament, especially in Isaiah, where it is associated with neglected or burned land and with something that can be consumed by fire. In some English renderings, “for” appears alongside the word as a connective, but it is not the thing named by the Hebrew term. Its normal sense is therefore a troublesome thorny growth rather than a person or abstract idea.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “sun,” referring to the bright heavenly body that gives daylight and marks the passing of the day. It is a noun used throughout the Old Testament, appearing 134 times in 127 verses. The word can be used in ordinary descriptions of daylight and time, as well as references to the sun’s place in the created order. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word expresses a limited idea whose exact sense depends on its context. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Lamentations 1:14, and serves as the predicate in that verse. The available lexical information does not provide a gloss, short definition, or approved fallback meaning, so a more specific English sense cannot be stated responsibly here. Its precise meaning must be understood from the actual wording and surrounding passage of Lamentations 1:14.

(call, be) bless(-ed, happy), go, guide, lead, relieve.

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses being “blessed.” It can describe a person or condition viewed in that way, functioning in Old Testament sentences as a predicate that declares such a state. It occurs 17 times in 15 verses across the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage context.

This Hebrew word is the name “Shetharboznai.” It is not given an explanatory definition in the available material; instead, it functions as a proper name preserved in English by transliteration. The name occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within four verses of Ezra, from Ezra 5:3 through Ezra 6:13. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies Shetharboznai rather than describing a general object, action, or quality.

e.t: This Hebrew word names a “mark”—a visible sign placed on or associated with someone. It occurs three times in the Old Testament corpus, including passages where the mark is spoken of as something God places or sets upon people. It also appears in Job in connection with a requested sign or written response, showing that its basic sense concerns an identifiable mark rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “wall,” referring to a constructed barrier or surrounding structure. It functions as a noun and appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Ezra. The word is used for something that can be built and described in terms of its size, making it a concrete term for a physical wall rather than an abstract boundary. Its occurrences are recorded in Ezra 5:3 and Ezra 5:9.

This Hebrew word refers to a “place.” It functions as a noun naming a location rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 30:33, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The available rendering supports the basic sense of a place, but the word’s single occurrence provides no broader range of uses to compare.

gl: a recurrence (of time or place); a reply (as returned)
d: a recurrence (of time or place); a reply (as returned)

e.t: This Hebrew word expresses “return”—the act or point of coming back. It is used in the Old Testament for a return to a place, a renewed movement back, or the time when someone comes again. Its central idea is reversal of direction: leaving is followed by coming back. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is an occasional term rather than a frequent one. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.
